newsitem.title: UK: Beef worries turn British children veggies - study.
newsitem.headline: Beef worries turn British children veggies - study.

text.p: Thirty-eight percent of four to 11-year-olds in Britain are avoiding eating beef and one in five is avoiding most meat, the Vegetarian Society said on Tuesday.
The report follows widespread concern in Britain that BSE, or mad cow disease, can be passed from infected cattle to humans through the food chain.
"I don't eat beef now because of mad cow disease," one seven-year-old boy told the study.
"To get such a high figure for such a young proportion of the population is quite dramatic," Stephen Connor, communications manager of the Vegetarian Society, told Reuters.
The report showed only three percent of the children were strict vegetarians, compared to an average of seven percent amongst adults.
But most people become vegetarian in their teens and these figures would indicate an increase in the national average a few years down the line, it said.
"Almost a quarter of that age group (children) were avoiding meat. That shows they'll be comfortable with a vegetarian diet in the future," Connor said.
The report was based on a sample of 973 parents with a total of 1,480 children. It showed the majority of parents agreed that a vegetarian child would be as healthy as a meat-eating child.
